Q: C standard: Can successful fgets still set the EOF indicator? A:

C standard: Can successful fgets() still set the EOF*3 indicator?

Yes.

This happens when fgets(buf, n, stream) reads at least 1 character and the encounters end-of-file before reading a total of n-1 non-'\n' characters. See also @dbush

... one should only call feof() (and ferror()) once the return value of an I/O function actually indicated failure.

The 'should' idea is about right.

When fgets() returns non-NULL:

  1. Some characters read and an input error did not occur.

  2. *1

When fgets() returns NULL:

  1. An input error just occurred*2. Often this occurs on the first read attempt, yet may occur after a successful read of several characters.

  2. If the stream's end-of-file indicator is set. This usually means this is no more characters to be read, yet some streams will have more data after earlier reporting end-of-file.

  3. If the stream's end-of-file indicator is not set yet the first attempt to read a character results in an-end-fil file.

  4. *1

Use feof() first before ferror()

*1
Invalid buffer or stream pointers, closed stream or pathological cases of n <= 0, are also potential cases.

*2
Note that if ferror() is set, that unto itself does not cause fgets() to return NULL. If the input error is persistent, than NULL will be returned due to another input error.

*3 There is no EOF indicator. There are stream's two end-of-file and error indicators. Several functions like fgetc() return an int EOF to indicate end-of-file or error. I'll assume OP meant "set the end-of-file indicator.

Q: How to make mysql2 gem to use new client version? A:

The warning you're seeing comes from the mysql2 gem checking the client library version it was compiled against — not the MySQL/MariaDB server version you connect to. Even though your server is MariaDB 10.5, the gem is linked to an older libmysqlclient (version 5.5.62) on the system.

Make sure you have the MariaDB or MySQL 8+ client library installed:

# For MariaDB (Debian/Ubuntu)
    sudo apt-get install libmariadb-dev
    
    # Or for MySQL 8+
    sudo apt-get install libmysqlclient-dev

Reinstall the gem so it compiles against the new library

    gem uninstall mysql2
    bundle install

Verify

Run your app again. The warning should be gone once `mysql2` is compiled against `libmysqlclient` 5.6.36+ or the MariaDB equivalent.

**Note:** If you cannot change the system library, you can point the gem to a specific client library path at install time:

    gem install mysql2 -- --with-mysql-dir=/usr/local/mysql

Q: How do professional programmers find logic efficiently? A:

Ex post facto, it's hard. It helps to try to mitigate them before they become a problem. One way to do that is write more unit tests; that way, you can be more confident that the individual pieces are free of logic errors before you integrate everything.

Q: How to resolve Unable to read data from the transport connection: net_io_connectionclosed error while sending email using SMTPClient A:

First Use Port = 587

Generally STARTTLS is required to send mail, Adding the Security Protocol Tls12 will help to resolve this issue.

Secondly test the stmp connection using powershell

$userName = 'username_here'
$password = 'xxxxxxxxx'
$pwdSecureString = ConvertTo-SecureString -Force -AsPlainText $password
$credential = New-Object -TypeName System.Management.Automation.PSCredential -ArgumentList $userName, $pwdSecureString

$sendMailParams = @{
    From = 'abc.com'
    To = 'xyz@gmail.com'
    Subject = 'Test SMTP'
    Body = 'Test SMTP'
    SMTPServer = 'smtp.server.com'
    Port = 587
    UseSsl = $true
    Credential = $credential
}

Send-MailMessage @sendMailParams

Thirdly If this send out the email, Add below code inside SmtpClient function:

System.Net.ServicePointManager.SecurityProtocol = SecurityProtocolType.Tls
                                      | SecurityProtocolType.Tls11
                                      | SecurityProtocolType.Tls12;

Q: How can I programmatically determine the capabilities of an optical drive in Win32 A:

You can use WMI to enumerate what Windows knows about a drive:

  • from the Win32_DiskDrive instance, you should be able to grab the the Win32_PhysicalMedia information for the physical media the drive uses
  • then use the MediaType property to get what media it uses (CD, CDRW, DVD, DVDRW, etc.)

Q: Is there a logical difference between putting a condition in the ON clause of an inner join versus the where clause of the main query? A:

Both versions return the same data.

Although this is true for an INNER JOIN, it is not true for OUTER JOINs.

Stylistically, there is a third possibility. In addition to your two, there is also:

select t1.field1, t2.field1
from (select t1.*
      from table1 t1
      where t1.boolfield = 1
     ) t1 inner join
     table2 t2
    on t1.id = t2.id

Which is preferable all depends on what you want to highlight, so you (or someone else) can later understand and modify the query. I often prefer the third version, because it emphasizes that the query is only using certain rows from the table -- the boolean condition is very close to where the table is specified.

In the other two cases, if you have a long query, it can be problematic to figure out what t1 really means. I think this is why some people prefer to put the condition in the ON clause. Others prefer the WHERE clause.
